draft.title: Primes and the fundamental theorem of arithmetic
card: Prime
a whole number greater than 1 with exactly two factors, 1 and itself. So 2, 3, 5, 7 and 11 are prime. 1 is not prime, and 2 is the only even prime.
Composite
a whole number greater than 1 that is not prime. It has a factor other than 1 and itself, so it can be broken into smaller factors.
Fundamental theorem
every whole number above 1 is a product of primes in exactly one way, apart from the order of the factors. For example, 60 = 2 × 30 = 2 × 2 × 15 = 2 × 2 × 3 × 5, which is 2² × 3 × 5.
Infinitely many

the list of primes never ends. Suppose there were a last prime. Multiply all the primes together and add 1. This number leaves remainder 1 when divided by any prime on the list, so it has a prime factor that is not on the list. This contradicts the supposed last prime.
draft.remember: Every whole number above 1 is built from primes in one way only, and the primes never run out.

a.q: What is the prime factorisation of 84?
a.why: 84 = 2 × 42 = 2 × 2 × 21 = 2 × 2 × 3 × 7, which is 2² × 3 × 7. The option 2 × 6 × 7 also multiplies to 84, but 6 is composite, so it is not a product of primes.
a.clue: Every factor in the answer must itself be prime.

b.q: Priya says the number 2 × 3 × 5 × 7 × 11 + 1 must be divisible by one of 2, 3, 5, 7 or 11. Which statement is correct?
opts: No, it leaves remainder 1 for each of them
Yes, because it is built from those primes
Yes, because every whole number above 1 is even
No, because it is itself always a prime number
b.why: The product 2 × 3 × 5 × 7 × 11 is divisible by each of these primes, so adding 1 leaves remainder 1 each time. The number is not divisible by any of them. It need not be prime, because it may have larger prime factors.
b.clue: Divide the product part by each prime, then think about the extra 1.

b.best: No, it leaves remainder 1 for each of them

problems.detail: The why says the number 'need not be prime, because it may have larger prime factors'. That holds in general, but this number, 2311, is itself prime. A student who checks could be confused. The why should say that such numbers are not always prime (for example 2×3×5×7×11×13 + 1 = 30031 = 59 × 509), while noting that 2311 happens to be prime.

check.summary: The card and both questions are correct. One small issue: the why for question b suggests the number may not be prime, but 2311 is in fact prime, so it should say plainly that such numbers are not always prime.

b.q: Priya says the number 2 × 3 × 5 × 7 × 11 + 1 must be divisible by one of 2, 3, 5, 7 or 11. Which statement is correct?
opts: No, it leaves remainder 1 when divided by each of them
Yes, because it is built from those primes
No, because it is odd, so no prime can divide it
Yes, because adding 1 keeps every factor of the product
b.why: The product 2 × 3 × 5 × 7 × 11 = 2310 is divisible by each of these primes, so 2311 leaves remainder 1 each time. Adding 1 breaks those factors rather than keeping them, and being odd only rules out 2. Numbers made this way are not always prime, since 2 × 3 × 5 × 7 × 11 × 13 + 1 = 30031 = 59 × 509, though 2311 happens to be prime.
b.clue: Divide the product part by each prime, then think about the extra 1.
